doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Advice to a grandson who wants to be a musician
summary: Harper says he had no plan B, but today there are fewer opportunities and more players than audience.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Oh them are all ages. I’ve got grandkids now. I’ve got six grandkids. But I’ve got kids from — the oldest I think is 30, so from 30 down.
If your grandson came to you when he’s like let’s say 12, 13 years old and says, “I want to be a musician.” What do you say to him?

You know that’s the thing. Over the years that has changed. And I don’t think it’s just because I’ve gotten older but I think the times have changed. Because when I was coming up, I mean people still said the same thing to me, but I think it was for a different reason, because I don’t think they saw what this was going to be like now. But even like some © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

other family members, if you said you were going to be a musician or you said you wanted to be an athlete or something, everybody always told you well look, “have your back-up plan.” It was always that when you go to school major in this. And my thoughts then were look there’s not going to be a back-up plan. This is what I’m going to do and I’m going to make it work and I’m going to succeed. I’m not thinking about Plan B. Nowadays I don’t know if I could really say that, you know, I mean tell my kids that. Because I would say it’s just so different. The opportunities that were there for me, I don’t really see those opportunities right now for aspiring musicians. Like I say this, I mean I can’t tell somebody well if you go to school and you do this and that I’m going to introduce you to so-and-so and you’ll be able to go out and do four years with Betty Carter or you can get with Art Blakey, you know, and they’ll take you on tour. Right now that’s not in place.
And at the same time the universities are graduating a lot more players that are trying to get —

We’re all trying to work. There’s a lot more players, there’s probably more players than there is audience And that’s until we work on that aspect of it, until we find ways to start replenishing the audience. But this is like anything else, supply and demand. If we can get the demand up then maybe we’ll get some other business owners and other people saying you know what? I’m going to open up a spot here, or I’m going to put a club back here. But right now I see too many clubs open up and fall by the wayside. Too many venues are suffering because they’re not able to make the kind of money off promoting jazz music.
